questions.title: What is the practical difference between 'de novo' review and 'substantial evidence' in trademark appeals?
questions.question_body: In Section II, the court states it reviews the Board’s legal conclusions 'de novo' but its findings of fact for 'substantial evidence.' As a student, I'm struggling to see how this affects the outcome of the DuPont factors. If a factor is a 'question of law' based on 'findings of relevant underlying facts,' which standard applies to the final decision on that specific factor?

questions.title: Under Section 2(d) of the Lanham Act, does 'likelihood of confusion' require proof of actual consumer confusion?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that the Board sustained the opposition because 'confusion is likely.' Based on the text, does the plaintiff (CC Serve) have to prove that a specific customer was actually confused between the two brands, or is the court looking at a hypothetical scenario of what a typical consumer might think?

questions.title: How did the court justify the finding that 'credit card services' and 'banking and financing services' are 'legally identical'?
questions.question_body: In Section III.A, Apex argued that they are not directly competitive because CC Serve manages programs for banks rather than providing banking services itself. However, the court affirmed the Board's finding of similarity. Can someone explain the court's logic regarding the dictionary definitions of 'banking' and 'finance' in this context? Why did the court include 'counseling' and 'monitoring' as part of the service definition?

questions.title: Why was the Board's limitation of the 'relevant public' to only credit card consumers considered a legal error under the sixth DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: This is the most confusing part of the ruling. The Board had already decided in the second factor that the services were 'highly similar' (even 'legally identical'). Why did the court rule that the Board was then required to use that same broad scope when looking at third-party marks in the sixth factor? Why can't the Board use a narrower scope for 'similar marks' than it did for 'similarity of services'?

questions.title: What is the legal connection between the sixth DuPont factor (crowded field) and the first DuPont factor (commercial impression)?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the Board's finding on the first factor (similarity of marks) simply because it vacated the sixth factor (number of similar marks). I don't fully understand the link. How does the existence of many similar marks in the marketplace (Factor 6) change the 'commercial impression' or 'connotation' of a mark (Factor 1) enough to warrant a remand?

questions.title: How does the 'narrow scope of protection' for a weak mark affect the likelihood of confusion analysis?
questions.question_body: In Section III.B, the court discusses how a 'crowded' field suggests a mark is 'relatively weak' and entitled to a 'narrow scope of protection.' If a mark is found to be weak/narrowly protected, does that make it *more* likely or *less* likely that a court will find a likelihood of confusion with a similar mark?
